h1: Planning a beer trip to Belgium for a first visit
title: Planning a First Beer Trip to Belgium | Craft Beer School
desc: How to plan a first beer trip to Belgium from India: where to base yourself, which styles to try, how to pace strong beers and what to book ahead.
teaser: Belgium is small, its beers are strong and the trains are good. Plan around those three facts.
standfirst: Belgium packs an extraordinary range of beer into a country you can cross by train in a few hours. Here is how we would plan a first visit: the bases, the styles, the pacing and the bookings.
sections: Belgium is small, so base yourself well

You can cross Belgium by train in about three hours, which changes how you plan. There is no need to move hotels every night. Pick one or two bases and take day trips. Brussels works for lambic country to the south-west and for easy connections everywhere. Bruges or Ghent work for West Flanders and its strong ales. Antwerp suits a city break with good beer bars.

Trains in Belgium are frequent and simple to use. You do not need a car. With beers this strong you should not want one. Indian passport holders need a Schengen visa, so start that process well before you book anything you cannot cancel.

Belgium is famous for range rather than a single style. A first trip should cover a few families:

  • Lambic and gueuze: spontaneously fermented beers from around Brussels, tart and dry.
  • Trappist and abbey beers: dubbels, tripels and quadrupels, many between 6 and 11% ABV.
  • Saison: dry, peppery farmhouse ales from Wallonia.
  • Flanders red and oud bruin: sour, barrel-aged beers from the west.
  • Witbier: a cloudy wheat beer with coriander and orange peel.

Write down five beers you have read about and want to taste fresh. That list gives the trip a shape.

Lambic is brewed in and around Brussels, especially in the Pajottenland and the Senne valley to the south-west. The wort is left to cool in open, shallow vessels called coolships so wild yeast and bacteria from the air can start fermentation. It then matures in barrels for one to three years. Because the coolship needs cold nights, lambic brewing traditionally runs only in the cooler months.

Cantillon in Brussels is the best-known working lambic brewery that welcomes visitors. Check its own site for visiting days and times before you go. Several lambic blenders and cafés in the towns south-west of the city are worth a day trip by train.

This is where first-time visitors come unstuck. A Belgian tripel at 8 to 9% ABV served in a 330 ml goblet carries well over twice the alcohol of a standard lager. Three of those in an afternoon is a lot.

Plan for it. Eat proper meals. Drink a glass of water with every beer. Order smaller pours where a bar offers them and share bottles. Many cafés serve beer in the brewery's own branded glass, which also means you can see how much is in it. Two or three thoughtful beers you remember beat seven you do not. Our guide to why the first and last sip taste different explains why slow drinking also tastes better.

A Belgian beer café often has a menu running to dozens or even hundreds of beers. Do not panic. Ask the staff. They usually know the list well and will suggest something based on what you like. Table service is common; you order at the table and settle up at the end.

Look at the glass. Many beers come in their own branded glass and staff take that seriously. Our guide on why Belgian breweries give each beer its own glass has the background. Snacks such as cheese cubes with celery salt are a common pairing.

Here is one shape that works for a first visit, based in Brussels and then Bruges or Ghent:

  • Day one: arrive, rest and visit one good beer café in Brussels. Keep it to two or three beers.
  • Day two: lambic. A brewery or blender visit in the morning, then a gueuze café in the afternoon.
  • Day three: move to Bruges or Ghent by train. Explore on foot and try a Flanders red.
  • Day four: a day trip for Trappist or abbey beers, with a driver or a tour so nobody drives.
  • Day five: a quiet morning, a shop for bottles to take home and the train to the airport.

That is roughly two styles a day, which is plenty. Leave one evening free. You will want it.
What to book before you fly

• The Schengen visa, with enough time for appointments.
  • Hotels in your one or two bases, close to the station.
  • Any brewery visits that need reservations. Many small breweries open to the public only on set days.
  • A rough day plan that leaves gaps. The best beer you find may be in a café you walked past.

Late spring and early autumn are comfortable for walking between cafés. Winter is cold but cosy. Some strong seasonal beers appear then.

The trip is a rare chance to taste beers fresh, close to where they were made. Keep a short note for each: style, ABV, aroma, flavour and one word for how it finished. You will be surprised how much blurs together otherwise.

The difference between a good beer trip and a great one is often what you can pick out in the glass. Knowing the reference notes for Belgian yeast esters, phenols and Brettanomyces makes every café visit sharper.

Your first step: pick your one or two bases this week and check Schengen visa appointment availability before you book flights.
faqs: Do I need a car for a beer trip in Belgium?
No. Belgian trains are frequent and the country is small, so one or two bases with day trips by train works well. It also means nobody has to drive after drinking.
Many are strong. Tripels are often 8 to 9% ABV and quadrupels around 10% or more, so pace yourself, eat and drink water alongside.
When is the best time to visit Belgium for beer?
Spring and early autumn are comfortable for walking between cafés. Lambic breweries traditionally brew in the cooler months.
